title: What are the Schema Registry compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, NONE), how do they let producers and consumers deploy independently, and why does adding a new required field break compatibility unless you give it a default (so old data can still be read)?
shortTitle: Schema Registry compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, NONE) and why defaults matter
keyPoints: BACKWARD (the default) means a consumer on the new schema can still read old data, so you upgrade consumers first.
FORWARD means a consumer on the old schema can still read new data, so you upgrade producers first.
FULL requires both backward and forward compatibility, allowing only the safest changes like adding or removing fields with defaults.
NONE disables checks entirely and should be avoided in production banking systems.
Adding a required field (no default) breaks BACKWARD compatibility because old records have no value for it.
Transitive variants (BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL_TRANSITIVE) check against all previous versions, not just the latest.
The CI pipeline should validate schema compatibility at build time using the schema-registry-maven-plugin.

s1_definition.oneliner: Compatibility modes let producers and consumers upgrade independently, and a new field is only safe to add if it has a default so old data remains readable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **BACKWARD** -- a consumer using the new schema can read data written with the previous schema; safe changes are deleting a field or adding a field with a default; upgrade consumers first.
- **FORWARD** -- a consumer using the old schema can read data written with the new schema; safe changes are adding a field or deleting a field that had a default; upgrade producers first.
- **FULL** -- both backward and forward hold simultaneously, so only the safest changes pass: adding or removing fields that have defaults.
- **NONE** -- disables compatibility checking entirely, allowing any change, which is dangerous in production.
- **Transitive variants** -- BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FORWARD_TRANSITIVE, and FULL_TRANSITIVE check against all previous versions, not just the latest, which matters when consumers may read very old data.
- **Required field rule** -- a field without a default is required; adding it breaks BACKWARD compatibility because old data has no value for it and no default to fall back on.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps changing the transfer form. BACKWARD compatibility means a clerk trained on the new form can still read all the old filled forms in the archive. FORWARD means a clerk trained on the old form can still read a new form someone just filled in. FULL means both clerks can read both forms. NONE means nobody checks and chaos is allowed. If the new form adds a mandatory currency box but every old archived form left it blank, the new clerk is stuck. The fix is to print INR as the default in that box, so when the box is blank the clerk assumes INR and keeps working.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Schema Evolution with BACKWARD Compatibility

  v1 schema          v2 schema (adds currency with default)
  ┌────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ accountId  │     │ accountId               │
  │ amount     │     │ amount                  │
  │ type       │     │ type                    │
  │            │     │ currency (default: INR) │
  └────────────┘     └─────────────────────────┘
        │                       │
        │    Old record         │   New consumer reads old record
        │    (no currency)      │   currency = INR (from default)
        ▼                       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          Schema Registry                  │
  │  Subject: transfers-value                 │
  │  Mode   : BACKWARD                        │
  │                                           │
  │  v1 registered   ✓                        │
  │  v2 registered   ✓ (compatible)           │
  │  v2 without default  ✗ (rejected!)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Schema Registry compatibility modes are the rules the registry enforces when a new schema version is registered, and they let producers and consumers evolve on their own schedules without breaking each other. BACKWARD, the default, means a consumer on the new schema can still read messages written with the old schema, so you upgrade consumers first. FORWARD means a consumer on the old schema can read messages written with the new schema, so you upgrade producers first. FULL requires both directions, and NONE turns the checks off.

The subtle point interviewers probe is about required fields. In Avro, a field without a default is required. If you add a required field, a consumer reading an older record that predates the field has no value and no default, so decoding fails and the registry rejects it. The fix is to give the new field a default. At National Bank of India, when Rajesh needed to add a currency field, the first attempt made it required and the registry rejected it immediately, which saved a production incident. He added a default of INR and it registered cleanly.

Pankaj always validates compatibility in the CI pipeline through the schema-registry-maven-plugin, so a bad schema fails the build instead of failing a consumer in production. The deployment order depends on the mode, and transitive variants matter when consumers replay from the beginning of a topic.

Remember one sentence: compatibility modes turn schema evolution from a risky big-bang release into a safe, independent process, and a new field is only safe if it has a default so old data can still be decoded.
